# `every_systemd_unit`

`every_systemd_unit` watches every systemd unit on the node at once:
services, timers, mounts, and every other kind of unit. The check is healthy
while systemd lists no failed unit. Each unit that systemd reports as
`failed` is its own incident, with its own alert and its own recovery. MMWatchdog
asks systemd with `systemctl list-units --state=failed`.

The check needs no list of the units to watch, so it also covers a unit that
nobody thought of. `every_systemd_unit` also covers a unit that is stopped
most of the time and must never fail, such as the unit of a scheduled job.
A scheduled job's unit is `inactive` between runs, so a
[`systemd_unit_state`](systemd_unit_state.md) check cannot watch the
scheduled job's unit. Use `systemd_unit_state` for a unit
that must run all the time. Write the continuously running unit into the
`every_systemd_unit` check's `systemd_units_to_ignore`.

## Inputs

- `fail_when` (`a_systemd_unit_has_failed`; required): The check fails while a systemd unit has failed; write a_systemd_unit_has_failed, the only value.
- `systemd_units_to_ignore` (list_of_strings; required): The units whose failure the check leaves out, each with its kind, such as myapp.service or backup.timer. An empty list leaves none out.

## When the check fails, and when it cannot check

The check reports a healthy run when systemd lists no failed unit outside
`systemd_units_to_ignore`. When systemd lists no failed unit at all, the
message is `no failed systemd units`. A failed unit in
`systemd_units_to_ignore` does not fail the check, and the message says so:
`no failed systemd units
(not counting 1 in systemd_units_to_ignore: myapp.service)`.

Each failed unit that the check does not ignore is one
[finding](../../changing-mmwatchdog/design/checks.md#findings) of the check, and each
finding is its own incident:

- **The check's message** counts and names the failed units, such as `2
  systemd units failed: backup.service, certbot.service`. A message names at
  most 20 units and counts the rest, such as `, and 3 more`.
- **The message of one unit** is `systemd unit backup.service failed
  (systemd result: exit-code)`, with the `Result` that systemd gives, or
  `systemd unit backup.service failed` when systemd gives none.
- **When systemd no longer lists the unit as failed,** the unit's message is
  `systemd unit backup.service is no longer failed`.
- **Each unit follows the check's settings by itself.** Its failing time
  starts at the first run that lists the unit as failed, and it ends when
  systemd has not listed the unit as failed for
  `recovered_after_healthy_for`. The failed unit's incident opens after
  `alert_after_failing_for`, so a second failed unit is announced while the
  first failed unit's incident is open. The check's `alert_severity`,
  `raise_to_sos_after_failing_for`, `send_alerts_only_to_destinations`, and
  the reminders of a destination apply to each unit's incident on its own.

- **The check itself** is failed while a unit has an open incident, and it
  has no failure incident of its own.

MMWatchdog cannot check, and the run is unknown, when it cannot ask systemd. The
message starts with `systemd inspection: MMWatchdog could not ask systemd for its
failed units:`. An unknown run belongs to the check, rather than to a unit.
After `alert_after_failing_for`, MMWatchdog sends one cannot-check alert
for the check, rather than one for each unit. Each unit's open incident
stays open. Time when MMWatchdog cannot ask systemd counts as healthy
time for no unit
([the failing time](../../how-to/decide-when-a-check-alerts.md)).

## Examples

### Alert for every failed unit

```yaml
# /etc/mmwatchdog/check_groups/failed_systemd_units.yml
check_groups:
  failed_systemd_units:
    check_every: 1m                               # ask systemd every minute
    time_limit_per_run: 5s
    alert_after_failing_for: 2m                   # alert for a unit that has been failed for 2 minutes
    recovered_after_healthy_for: 1m               # "recovered" when systemd has not listed the unit for 1 minute
    checks:
      machine_has_no_failed_systemd_unit:
        every_systemd_unit:
          fail_when: a_systemd_unit_has_failed
          systemd_units_to_ignore: [myapp.service]   # this unit has a check of its own
        alert_severity: warn
```

On the node `app-1`:

1. At 02:00 the nightly backup unit `backup.service` ends with exit status 1,
   and systemd reports it as `failed`.
2. At 02:02 MMWatchdog sends a `warn` alert for `backup.service`.
   The failure alert's title is `app-1:
   failed_systemd_units/machine_has_no_failed_systemd_unit: backup.service
   failed`. The failure alert's body starts with
   `systemd unit backup.service failed
   (systemd result: exit-code)`.
3. At 03:00 the unit `certbot.service` fails too. At 03:02 MMWatchdog sends a second
   alert, for `certbot.service`.
4. At 09:10 an operator repairs the backup and runs `backup.service` again.
   At 09:11 MMWatchdog sends the recovery notification for `backup.service`.
   The recovery notification's title is `app-1:
   failed_systemd_units/machine_has_no_failed_systemd_unit: backup.service
   is ok again`. The recovery notification's message is
   `systemd unit backup.service is no longer failed`. The incident of
   `certbot.service` stays open.

When `myapp.service` fails, `every_systemd_unit` sends nothing, because the
unit is in `systemd_units_to_ignore`. The unit's own `systemd_unit_state` check
sends its alert.

### What the commands show

`mmwatchdog status` shows the check with one line for each failed unit:

```text
failed_systemd_units/machine_has_no_failed_systemd_unit failed       2 systemd units failed: backup.service, certbot.service
  backup.service             failed       systemd unit backup.service failed (systemd result: exit-code)
  certbot.service            confirming_failure systemd unit certbot.service failed (systemd result: exit-code)
```

- In `mmwatchdog status --json` the check has `one_incident_for_each_finding: true`,
  and its own `failure_incident` never holds an incident. The check object's
  `findings` maps each unit to an entry with the fields of a check: `state`,
  `last_observation`, `failing_since`, and `failure_incident`.
  The `summary` has an `attention` entry for each unit with an open incident.
  Each attention entry's `finding` field holds
  the unit name.
- `mmwatchdog check-now` prints the failed units of that moment, one line for each,
  such as `Finding backup.service: systemd unit backup.service failed
  (systemd result: exit-code)`. In JSON, `mmwatchdog check-now` lists the
  currently failed units as `findings`. Each
  finding has an `id` field containing the unit name and a `message` field
  explaining the unit's failure.
- `mmwatchdog fleet NODE` on the hub shows each failed unit under its check.

### The validation warning for a unit with its own check

A unit with its own `systemd_unit_state` check belongs in
the `every_systemd_unit` check's `systemd_units_to_ignore`. Otherwise, a
failure of the unit with a `systemd_unit_state` check sends two alerts.
`mmwatchdog validate` and `mmwatchdog reload` name each unit with a
`systemd_unit_state` check missing from an `every_systemd_unit` check's
`systemd_units_to_ignore`. The configuration stays valid:

```text
$ mmwatchdog validate
Valid configuration: 2 check groups, 1 alert destination
An every_systemd_unit check alerts for every failed systemd unit outside the check's systemd_units_to_ignore list. The units listed below also have a systemd_unit_state check, so a unit failure would send two alerts. Add each listed unit to systemd_units_to_ignore:
  failed_systemd_units/machine_has_no_failed_systemd_unit: myapp.service is missing from systemd_units_to_ignore; myapp/myapp_service_is_running also checks the systemd unit
```

`mmwatchdog validate --json` lists the units missing from each
`every_systemd_unit` check's ignore list under
`systemd_units_missing_from_systemd_units_to_ignore`
([validation warnings](../commands.md#validation-warnings)). The warning
looks only at units with a `systemd_unit_state` check, not at units with
another check.

## How it works

1. At each run, MMWatchdog runs `systemctl list-units --state=failed --all --plain
   --full --no-legend --no-pager` on the node, as MMWatchdog itself. The
   `systemctl list-units` command lists failed units of every kind.
2. MMWatchdog reads the `ActiveState` and the `Result` of each listed unit with one
   `systemctl show` command. MMWatchdog leaves out a unit that stopped being
   failed after `systemctl list-units` and before `systemctl show`.
   When `systemctl show` gives no answer for a unit, the unit counts as
   failed, and the unit's message has no result.
3. MMWatchdog leaves out the units in `systemd_units_to_ignore` and reports each
   other unit as a finding, with the unit's name as the finding's `id`.

MMWatchdog changes nothing about a unit and never clears a failed state. A unit
stays failed in systemd until it runs again or someone runs `systemctl
reset-failed`.

**`systemd_units_to_ignore`** is required, so a reader sees at once whether
any unit is left out. `[]` leaves no unit out. Each entry is the full name of
a unit with its kind, such as `myapp.service` or `backup.timer`. An entry is
an exact name, not a pattern. The order of the entries does not matter.

**A changed check starts afresh.** `systemd_units_to_ignore` is part of the
check. A reload that changes the ignore list or removes the check closes
each failed unit's incident.
The incidents close without a recovery (`incident closed without
recovery`), like the incident of every changed check. A unit that is still
failed and not ignored gets a new incident after `alert_after_failing_for`.
A reload that only changes the order of the list changes nothing.

**Alerts name the unit.** Every alert about a unit puts the unit name after
the check name in the alert's title. The alert's message also names the
unit. The alert's event has the unit name as `finding`, as in webhook JSON
([title and body of an alert](../alert-format.md)).

`mmwatchdog validate` cannot know the unit's name, so its warning about long alert
titles counts the `every_systemd_unit` check's title without a unit.
When adding the unit name makes a title longer than 120 characters,
MMWatchdog shortens the title as MMWatchdog shortens other names in a title.

**In a fleet,** the hub groups the alerts of each unit by themselves.
`backup.service` failing on seven nodes becomes
`failed_systemd_units/machine_has_no_failed_systemd_unit: backup.service
failed on 7 nodes`. A different unit that fails in the minute of the
`backup.service` failure has separate messages
([alerts in a fleet](../../how-to/set-up-a-fleet.md#where-alerts-go-in-a-fleet)).
Each unit has its own MMHotline incident key, such as
`failed_systemd_units/machine_has_no_failed_systemd_unit: backup.service
failed`, so two failed units are two MMHotline incidents, and the recovery
of one resolves only its own ([`mmhotline`](mmhotline.md#what-it-sends)).

**One cause, one alert.** When an `every_systemd_unit` check is kept quiet
because a check named by `every_systemd_unit` fails, each failed unit is
kept quiet too.

When another check names the `every_systemd_unit` check as a cause, the
alert of each failed unit names the checks kept quiet
([one cause, one alert](../../how-to/stop-alerts-that-follow-another-failure.md)).

**Recovery actions.** A
[restart](../../how-to/restart-a-service-automatically.md#steps-to-restart-a-systemd-unit) or a
[recovery command](../../how-to/restart-a-service-automatically.md#steps-to-run-a-command-instead) that names the
`every_systemd_unit` check in `triggered_by_checks` counts the check's own
failing time, which lasts while systemd lists any unit as failed.
The check has no incident of its own, so a recovery command gets an empty
`MMWATCHDOG_INCIDENT_ID`.

## Errors and what they mean

| Message | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| `every_systemd_unit.fail_when: is required: The check fails while a systemd unit has failed; write a_systemd_unit_has_failed, the only value.` | Write `fail_when: a_systemd_unit_has_failed` below `every_systemd_unit`. |
| `every_systemd_unit.fail_when: expected one of a_systemd_unit_has_failed` | Use `a_systemd_unit_has_failed`, the only allowed value. |
| `check_groups.failed_systemd_units.checks.machine_has_no_failed_systemd_unit.every_systemd_unit.systemd_units_to_ignore: is required: the systemd units whose failure this check leaves out, such as [myapp.service], or [] to leave none out` | Write the list. `[]` leaves no unit out. |
| `...every_systemd_unit.systemd_units_to_ignore: expected distinct systemd unit names with their kind, such as [myapp.service, backup.timer]` | Write each unit once, with its kind after the last dot. A unit name may contain only letters, digits, and the characters `_@.:\-`, at most 255 characters. |
| `An every_systemd_unit check alerts for every failed systemd unit outside the check's systemd_units_to_ignore list. ...` (a validation warning) | Add each named unit to `systemd_units_to_ignore`. |
| `systemd inspection: MMWatchdog could not ask systemd for its failed units: ...` (unknown) | `systemctl` failed. The message contains the failed `systemctl` command's exit status and output. |

## Tested on

- **Go tests:**
  In `failed_units_test.go`, `TestFailedSystemdUnitsCheckAsksSystemd` checks
  units of every kind and omits a unit that stops being failed between
  `systemctl list-units` and `systemctl show`. The test also checks that
  ignored units are left out and named in the message. When systemd cannot
  be inspected, the test expects an unknown run.
  `TestEachFailedSystemdUnitIsItsOwnIncident` checks the example above
  minute by minute.

  More tests in `failed_units_test.go` cover each unit's lifecycle and
  delivery: `TestAFailedUnitFollowsTheChecksTimingsByItself`,
  `TestFailedUnitsWhileSystemdCannotBeAsked`, `TestFailedUnitsInMaintenance`,
  `TestFailedUnitsAreRaisedAndRemindedOfByThemselves`, `TestSystemdUnitsToIgnore`,
  `TestTheRecoveryOfAFailedUnitSaysThatTheUnitIsNoLongerFailed`,
  `TestFailedUnitsInStatusAcrossRestartAndReload`,
  `TestFailedUnitsTriggerARecoveryCommand`, `TestTheHubGroupsFailedUnitsByUnit`,
  `TestFailedUnitsHaveTheirOwnMMHotlineIncidents`, `TestFailedUnitsThroughTheHub`,
  and `TestRemindersOfTwoUnitsDoNotReplaceEachOther`.

  Quiet checks are covered by `onecause_test.go`:
  `TestAQuietCheckWithOneIncidentForEachFailedUnit` and
  `TestTheAlertOfEachFailedUnitNamesTheQuietChecks`.
  `TestFailedSystemdUnitsOnTheCommandLine` in `cmd/mmwatchdog/main_test.go`
  checks the text and JSON of the `mmwatchdog validate` warning. The command
  test also checks for one line per unit in `mmwatchdog status` and
  `mmwatchdog fleet NODE`.
- **Suites on real nodes:** the `resources` suite (`lifecycle.py`): real
  one-time units that fail. The suite verifies that an ignored failed unit
  does not fail the check. Two units fail in succession and get separate
  incidents. Each unit appears in the title, body, `mmwatchdog status`,
  `attention` list, and `mmwatchdog check-now --json`.

  A repaired unit recovers while the second unit's incident stays open,
  including across a restart of MMWatchdog. Adding a failed unit to
  `systemd_units_to_ignore` closes the unit's incident without a recovery.
  `mmwatchdog validate` warns about a unit with a dedicated
  `systemd_unit_state` check.

  The `fleet` suite (`fleet.py`): a failed unit on a joined node
  sends its alert and its recovery through the hub with the unit in the
  title, and the hub shows the unit under its check.
- The `resources` and `fleet` suites passed on
  [every target distribution](../../changing-mmwatchdog/testing.md#every-target-distribution).
  The [validation record](../../changing-mmwatchdog/validation.md) has the latest run.
- **Not tested on real nodes:** maintenance windows, reminders, increases
  of incident severity to `sos`, and the MMHotline keys of a unit's
  incident, which the Go tests cover; an `every_systemd_unit` check as a
  quiet check or as a cause of one cause, one alert, which the Go tests
  cover; a joined node that sends a unit's incident straight to MMHotline
  while the hub is down, which the Go tests cover; and many failed units at
  once. Each failed unit is its own alert, with no upper limit.

## Why it works this way

- **Each failed unit is its own incident.** A second failed unit is announced
  at once. Each repaired unit reports a separate
  recovery. One incident for the whole list would stay open from the first
  failure to the last repair and announce nothing in between.
- **`systemd_units_to_ignore` is required, and a unit with its own check is
  written into it.** A reader sees at once whether any unit is left out.
  Automatically ignoring units with dedicated checks would make
  `systemd_units_to_ignore: []` misleading, because an empty list means no
  unit is ignored.
- **A failed unit takes the alert severity of its check.** A reader sees the
  severity on the check itself, as for every alert. Two severities are two
  checks.
- **An unknown run is the check's, not a unit's.** MMWatchdog learned nothing about
  any unit, so it sends one cannot-check alert and leaves each open incident
  as it is.
- **MMWatchdog never clears a failed state.** systemd supervises the units, and MMWatchdog
  only observes them. A unit that stays failed stays visible.
- **One mechanism for findings.** The `every_systemd_unit` module and every
  module that reports several findings at once use one mechanism for
  findings. Findings behave alike in status, alerts, and
  the fleet.
